newsitem.title: USA: Durable goods orders up 4.6 percent in September.
newsitem.headline: Durable goods orders up 4.6 percent in September.

text.p: Orders for expensive manufactured goods unexpectedly jumped in September, the Commerce Department said Friday, as strong demand for aircraft more than erased a very weak showing in August.

The department said new orders for durable goods rose 4.6 percent, the largest increase in nearly four years, to a seasonally adjusted $174.1 billion after declining a revised 3.5 percent decline in August.

The increase far outstripped Wall Street estimates of a 2.0 percent rise. But analysts were quick to point out that the increase primarily reflected recent aircraft orders being lumped together in one month.
Previously, the department said that August orders had declined 3.2 percent.
Overall orders posted the largest increase since December, 1992.
"It's a stronger-than-expected figure, but when you look at the breakdown it's nothing remarkable ... mainly due to aircraft," said David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A. Inc.

Orders for durable goods, such as cars, planes and home appliances intended to last at least three years, are viewed by economists as a measure of the vitality of the manufacturing sector, a powerful influence on the overall economy.
Transportation equipment showed the largest increase last month, moving up 17.5 percent to $44.1 billion, with over half the increase accounted for by aircraft and parts.
Orders for electronic and other electrical equipment, which includes computers, were up in three of the last four months and rose 1.9 percent in September, after being down 5.2 percent in August.

"Love that computer industry," said First Union economist Joel Naroff. But he added that "while durable goods orders did increase sharply, it cannot be taken as a sign of renewed strong growth in the economy."

Evidence to back the idea that the economy is slowing came from the National Association of Realtors, which reported that sales of existing homes fell 2.9 percent in September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 4.02 million units from a revised 4.14 million units in August.
But while the durable goods numbers may not have been as strong as they appeared at first blush, they still showed a strong manufacturing sector, analysts said.
Daiwa Securities economist Michael Moran said orders have been showing a seesaw pattern in recent months, "but there has been an upward trend in these ups and downs."
The department said orders for industrial machinery and equipment fell 0.9 percent in the month, as did primary metals, which declined 1.7 percent after dropping 4.0 percent in August.

The manufacturing sector has been expanding in recent months, although it is generally believed that the economy is slowing from a very strong pace earlier in the year. The August and September durable goods figures demonstrate how highly volatile the sector can be on a month-to-month basis.

"The only surprise is in civilian aircraft, which is high as a result of Boeing's recent string of orders being lumped into one month," said Waldo Best, senior economist at BZW Securities Inc. "The overall number suggests goods production is still moderate and does not demand any immediate attention from the Fed."
The next meeting of the Federal Reserve's policy-setting Open Markets Committee is scheduled for Nov. 13.

The inflation-sensitive 30-year Treasury bond fell half a point immediately after the report was issued. But it later bounced back and climbed nearly half a point, pulling its yield down to 6.81 percent from 6.85 percent Thursday.
The department said defence capital goods orders also helped buoy the overall results, rising 7.9 percent, the fourth increase in the last five months, following a 2.0 percent rise in August.
Non-defence capital goods orders, an indicator of investment in new equipment by business, zoomed up 14.1 percent following a 10.4 percent retreat in August.
Shipments of durable goods, a measure of current demand in manufacturing industries, increased 1.4 percent after rising 0.4 percent in August.
